Mongolian grayling (Thymallus brevirostris) populations in the cold rivers of Mongolia exhibit several distinctive life-history traits that have been documented in recent field surveys. Maximum recorded total length in adults reaches approximately 65 centimeters [Li = approximately 65 centimeters], although FishBase lists a smaller typical value of 39 centimeters likely reflecting non-piscivorous forms that experience different growth constraints. Spawning adults are iteroparous and typically reproduce annually, with reproductive activity closely tied to thermal conditions in their native habitat. In a laboratory setting maintained at a stable water temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C], the maximum reproductive output was estimated at roughly 6000 eggs per spawning season [Ri = roughly 6000 eggs per spawning season] and a single spawning event per year [F_R_i = single spawning event per year], a value derived from closely related congeneric species. Female egg production is continuous during the reproductive season, and the maximum daily rate translates to a substantial annual fecundity given the extended spawning window.

At a constant incubation temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C], the yolk-sac larva emerges through eclosion after approximately 15 days [ab = approximately 15 days], a developmental duration typical for cold-water thymallids that reflects the slow metabolic rates associated with low thermal regimes. The newly emerged alevin is entirely lecithotrophic and relies on endogenous yolk reserves during this early endotrophic phase. The wet weight at birth for these prolarvae is extremely low, estimated at 0.0048 grams [Wwb = 0.0048 grams], a value based on the egg diameter of related coregonids. This minute initial mass reflects the small egg size characteristic of many salmoniform fishes and imposes a tight energetic budget during the critical period of first exogenous feeding. Following yolk-sac resorption, the exotrophic transition marks the onset of active feeding, after which juvenile growth becomes heavily dependent on invertebrate prey availability.

Sexual maturation in Mongolian grayling is closely coupled with body size, as is common among northern freshwater fishes. The total length at puberty is estimated at 33 centimeters [Lp = 33 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds to the onset of gonad maturation and gametogenesis. At this length, individuals transitioning to reproductive maturity have a wet weight at puberty of approximately 430 grams [Wwp = approximately 430 grams], a mass that represents a considerable somatic investment before the first spawning event. The relationship between length and weight in this species follows a typical power-law growth trajectory, with individuals accumulating significant lipid reserves to support the energetic demands of vitellogenesis and spawning migration. Puberty generally occurs after several years of juvenile growth, during which the fish must navigate seasonal feeding opportunities and harsh winter conditions.

The ultimate wet weight, representing the asymptotic adult body mass, has been estimated at approximately 3130 grams [Wwi = approximately 3130 grams] based on the species-specific length-weight regression. This maximum mass is achieved only by the largest individuals, which likely represent older, piscivorous adults that have sustained high feeding rates over many seasons. Such large body sizes are relatively uncommon in contemporary populations, potentially due to fishing pressure that truncates the age structure. Under the thermal regime typical of their natal streams (9 °C [T = 9 °C]), maximum lifespan in the wild has been documented at around 5110 days [am = around 5110 days], or approximately 14 years. This extended longevity is consistent with the general pattern observed in cold-adapted salmonids, where slow metabolic rates and delayed senescence are common. Achieving such an advanced age requires successful navigation of multiple spawning seasons and avoidance of both natural predators and anthropogenic mortality sources.

Comparative studies among Thymallus species reveal that Mongolian grayling occupies a relatively slow-paced life-history position within the genus. The species' body size at sexual maturation, at 33 centimeters [Lp = 33 centimeters], represents a substantial proportion of its maximum attainable length of 65 centimeters [Li = 65 centimeters], indicating a life-history strategy that prioritizes somatic growth before the onset of reproductive investment. The wet weight at puberty of 430 grams [Wwp = 430 grams] is only about one-seventh of the ultimate body mass of 3130 grams [Wwi = 3130 grams], suggesting that considerable growth potential remains after maturation. This pattern is typical of iteroparous fishes that continue to increase fecundity with age.
